transcript.speaker: ai
transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, I appear on behalf of the Complainant, a consumer who placed her trust — and her personal data — in the hands of a ride-hailing application, only to have that trust systematically and deliberately violated. The facts are stark and uncontested: the Respondent company shared my client's phone number and live location with third-party advertisers, without her knowledge, without her consent, and in direct contradiction of their own published privacy policy. This is not a technical breach. This is a fundamental assault on a constitutionally protected right.

Your Lordship, the Supreme Court in **K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India** (docid: 1199182) — decided by a nine-judge bench, the highest constitutional authority available — held unequivocally that informational privacy is a facet of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21, and that any processing of personal data must satisfy the twin pillars of **consent and purpose limitation**. The Respondent's own privacy policy was the very instrument by which consent was solicited and defined. By sharing my client's phone number and live location with advertisers — a purpose nowhere disclosed or consented to — the Respondent violated both pillars simultaneously. There is no ambiguity here; the Respondent's conduct fails the proportionality test on its face.

Your Lordship, I further submit that the **polluter-pays principle** articulated in **Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India** (docid: 7012009) applies with full force in the data-privacy context. Just as an industrial enterprise cannot externalize the cost of the damage it causes onto innocent citizens, a data-processing enterprise cannot profit from the unauthorized exploitation of personal data while leaving the victim to bear the consequences — harassment, targeted manipulation, and the chilling effect on her freedom of movement. The financial and remedial cost of this breach must be borne entirely by the party that caused it: the Respondent.

Finally, Your Lordship, this Court must note that the Respondent is not a passive actor. It is a sophisticated commercial enterprise that drafted its own privacy policy, built the technical infrastructure to share data, and chose to monetize my client's information without authorization. The principle of absolute and non-delegable duty recognized in **M.C. Mehta v. Union of India** (docid: 6033120) — that an enterprise engaged in an inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute duty to the community — is instructive. The collection and real-time sharing of live location data is precisely such an activity; the potential for harm, including stalking, physical danger, and identity theft, is self-evident. The Respondent cannot hide behind contractual fine print or technical complexity. We seek a declaration of liability, mandatory deletion of unlawfully shared data, and substantial compensatory relief for my client. I am grateful, Your Lordship.

transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, I appear for the Respondent ride-hailing company, and I must respectfully submit that my learned friend's case, while rhetorically forceful, rests on several critical infirmities that this Court must examine before any liability is fastened upon my client.

First, on the invocation of **K.S. Puttaswamy** (docid: 1199182): my learned friend conveniently omits that the nine-judge bench's proportionality framework was articulated in the context of **State action** — restrictions imposed by the government on fundamental rights. The Respondent is a private commercial entity. The horizontal application of Article 21 against a private party in a consumer dispute requires a far more careful doctrinal bridge than my learned friend has constructed. Puttaswamy itself acknowledges that any restriction must satisfy "legality, legitimate State aim, and proportionality" — language directed at State actors. Before this Court proceeds on a constitutional footing, my learned friend must first establish the evidentiary foundation: **where is the forensic proof** that data was actually shared, with whom, and at whose direction within the Respondent's organisation? The complaint as framed asserts this as "uncontested fact," yet no technical audit report, no server log, no third-party advertiser affidavit has been placed on record. The burden of proof lies squarely with the Complainant, and it has not been discharged.

Second, the transplantation of the **polluter-pays principle** from **Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action** (docid: 7012009) into a data-privacy consumer dispute is a category error. That principle was evolved in the context of physical environmental harm — chemical effluents, tangible ecological damage — where causation and the identity of the responsible party were established on record. My learned friend cannot simply borrow a liability standard from environmental law and apply it wholesale to an alleged data breach without demonstrating that the same doctrinal logic governs. The principle "informs liability and compensation analysis across regulatory disputes," yes — but it does not substitute for proof of the primary wrong.

Third, and critically, Your Lordship must note the **absence of specific statutory authority** in this complaint. My learned friend has not pointed to any provision of the Information Technology Act or any notified rule under it that this Court is being asked to enforce in these proceedings. The privacy policy is a contractual document; any breach of it is, at its highest, a contractual or tortious claim requiring proof of actual damage. Until Parliament enacts comprehensive data-protection legislation — a gap that, as this Court knows from **Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan** (docid: 4087220), courts may fill with guidelines but cannot fill with punitive liability against private parties without a principled basis — the Complainant's remedy must be measured and proportionate, not open-ended. I urge Your Lordship to require strict proof before proceeding further.

transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, my learned friend has raised two objections — one doctrinal, one evidentiary — and I shall demolish both in turn.

On the question of horizontal application, my learned friend argues that *Puttaswamy* (docid: 1199182) speaks only to State action. With respect, that is a selective and impoverished reading of a nine-judge bench. The Court in *Puttaswamy* held that informational privacy is a **facet of the right to life and personal liberty** — it is not a right that evaporates the moment one steps into a commercial relationship with a private entity. More critically, the Court expressly identified **consent and purpose limitation** as "central to lawful processing of personal data." The Respondent is not being prosecuted under Article 21 as a State actor; it is being held to account for **contractually and constitutionally recognised privacy norms** that it voluntarily undertook to honour in its own published privacy policy. When a company publishes a policy promising data protection and then does the precise opposite, it cannot hide behind the State-action doctrine. The constitutional standard illuminates the normative floor; the breach of that floor in a consumer relationship is actionable before this Forum.

On the evidentiary challenge, Your Lordship, my learned friend demands forensic logs and server audits before liability can even be considered. I submit that this argument inverts the proper analysis at this stage. The **Respondent alone possesses** the server logs, the API integration records, the advertiser contracts, and the data-sharing agreements. The information asymmetry here is total and deliberate. It is a well-recognised principle — and one this Court may apply in equity — that where evidence lies exclusively within the defendant's control, an adverse inference is permissible when that evidence is withheld. My client has placed on record the privacy policy, the contradiction between its promises and the reported conduct, and the harm suffered. The burden now shifts to the Respondent to produce its own records and demonstrate that no unauthorised sharing occurred. Silence on that score is not a neutral fact.

Finally, Your Lordship, even if this Court were to find the constitutional bridge imperfect, the principle drawn from *Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action* (docid: 7012009) — that the party responsible for harm must bear its financial cost — applies with full force here. The Respondent profited commercially from sharing my client's data with advertisers. The financial benefit of that wrongdoing flowed to the Respondent; the harm — exposure of live location and phone number to unknown third parties — fell entirely upon my client. That is precisely the asymmetry the polluter-pays principle was designed to correct, and its application to a data-sharing enterprise that externalises privacy harm onto consumers is not a transplant; it is a natural extension of a compensatory principle that this Court has consistently endorsed across regulatory contexts.
